opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd start by saying that "ready" isn't a property of the model alone. It's a property of the model in a particular setting, with particular people, doing a particular job. A lot of the evaluation culture in machine learning grew up around benchmarks: a fixed dataset and a single number you try to push up. That's been useful for measuring progress, but it maps poorly onto questions like "should a clinician rely on this to draft patient messages?" or "should a ninth grader use this as a tutor?"

So the first thing I try to do is ask what the deployment actually looks like. Who is using the system? What decision or action does its output feed into? What does a failure cost, and who bears that cost? In health care, a confident wrong answer about a drug interaction is very different from a slightly awkward summary of a visit note. In education, a model that gives the right answer but short-circuits the student's learning can be a failure, even though a standard accuracy metric would call it a success. The construct you care about, whether that's patient safety, clinical utility, or actual learning, is often not what the benchmark is measuring. Being careful about that gap between what we measure and what we mean is, I think, the core of the problem.

The second piece is that these evaluations have to be much more contextual and much more ongoing than we're used to. Some practical implications:

- **Measure variability, not just averages.** You want to know how performance shifts across patient populations, across languages and dialects, across students with different backgrounds. An aggregate score can hide the fact that the system works well for some groups and poorly for exactly the people who are already underserved.

- **Evaluate the human plus the model, not the model alone.** In both domains the model rarely acts alone. A doctor or teacher is in the loop, and how people over-trust or under-trust the system matters a lot. Sometimes a model that looks great in isolation makes the overall team worse.

- **Worry about contamination and saturation.** Models have been trained on huge swaths of the internet, which probably include versions of standard medical exam questions. A high score on a licensing-style exam tells you surprisingly little about whether the model can handle a messy real-world case.

- **Keep monitoring after deployment.** Models get updated, user behavior changes, and the distribution of questions drifts. A one-time certification isn't enough. You need something closer to post-market surveillance.

The last thing I'd emphasize is that this can't be done by machine learning people alone. Clinicians, educators, patients, and students need to help define what good looks like, because they understand the failure modes in ways we often don't. The measurement science has a lot to offer here: thinking about validity, reliability, and what a score actually licenses you to conclude. To me, the exciting research agenda is bringing that rigor to AI evaluation so that "ready" becomes a claim we can actually defend, rather than a vibe based on a leaderboard.

r001.rationale: The response says fixed-dataset benchmarks map poorly onto health care and education readiness questions, and explains that benchmark measures may miss concerns such as patient safety and actual learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing I'd say is that "ready" is doing a lot of work in that question, and part of what my group has been trying to do is unpack it. Because when people ask whether a model is ready for health care or education, they usually have a benchmark score in mind, and I think the benchmark score is almost never the thing that actually determines readiness.

Let me give you a concrete example. In the medical space, there's been a lot of excitement about models passing medical licensing exams, USMLE-style questions. And that's a real signal, I don't want to dismiss it. But a licensing exam is a proxy for a much richer set of competencies that a clinician has, and the exam was designed with the assumption that the test-taker is a human who went through medical training. So when a model passes it, we've learned something about the model, but we haven't learned that the model has the competencies the exam was meant to certify. The proxy and the target have come apart.

So the way I think about it is in a few layers. The first layer is capability: can the model do the task at all, on the distribution we care about, and does that distribution actually look like the deployment setting? A lot of medical benchmarks are drawn from textbooks or exam prep material, and real patient interactions look nothing like that. Questions are messier, information is incomplete, people describe symptoms in ways that don't map cleanly onto clinical vocabulary.

The second layer is what I'd call robustness and reliability, and this is where I think a lot of the action is. It's not enough that the model is right on average. In a high-stakes setting, you care about the tails. You care about whether performance is consistent across subpopulations, because health care and education both have long histories of systems that work well for the majority group and poorly for everyone else. And you care about whether the model knows when it doesn't know. A model that's ninety percent accurate but confidently wrong on the other ten percent is a very different object from one that's ninety percent accurate and flags the cases it's unsure about. In a clinical workflow, the second one is usable and the first one may be dangerous.

The third layer, and this is the one that I think is most underappreciated, is that readiness is a property of the whole sociotechnical system, not the model. The question isn't "is the model ready," it's "is this model, used in this way, by these people, with these safeguards, ready." The same model could be perfectly appropriate as a tool that helps a nurse draft a discharge summary that gets reviewed, and completely inappropriate as something that talks directly to patients with no oversight. In education it's similar. A model that's great as a tutor for a motivated student who's checking its work might be harmful for a struggling student who takes everything it says at face value, or who learns to offload the thinking entirely.

So when we evaluate, I try to push people toward evaluating the deployment, not the artifact. That means being explicit about the use case, measuring the things that matter for that use case, including the failure modes and who bears the cost of those failures, and ideally doing some of that measurement in situ, with the actual users, rather than purely on static benchmarks.

And I'll say the honest thing, which is that this is hard and expensive and the field has mostly not done it. We've gotten very good at leaderboard-style evaluation because it's cheap and it scales. Evaluating whether something is actually ready for a hospital or a classroom requires domain expertise, it requires working with institutions, it often requires something that looks more like a clinical trial than a benchmark run. I think that's where we need to go, but I'd be lying if I said we had a mature methodology for it right now. What we have is a growing recognition that the benchmark number is not the answer, and that's at least a start.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark scores and textbook or exam-based tests may not reflect real health care or education settings, and argues for evaluating the specific deployment and its concerns.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is, ready for what? Health care and education are both very broad. Helping a clinician draft a note is a different task from recommending a treatment, and helping a student practice a concept is different from grading an exam. The evidence we need should depend on the particular use and the consequences of getting it wrong.

Benchmarks can be useful, but they’re only part of that evidence. A model might do well on medical exam questions without improving clinical decisions. Similarly, giving correct answers to homework questions doesn’t necessarily mean it helps students learn. We need evaluations that measure the outcomes we actually care about, with the people who will use these systems.

I’d also want to understand what the averages hide. Where does the model fail? Who does it fail for? Can users recognize those failures, and does the system appropriately express uncertainty? Putting a human in the loop doesn’t automatically solve those problems; we have to evaluate how the human and the model work together.

So I think of readiness as a claim about a specific system in a specific setting, supported by evidence. And that evaluation needs to continue after deployment, because how people use the system can change what its risks and benefits look like.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark performance alone may not establish readiness: medical exam scores may not reflect better clinical decisions, and homework accuracy may not show improved learning. It calls for evaluating outcomes in the specific use setting.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to ask, ready for what? Health care and education are both very broad. A model that helps a clinician draft a note is doing something quite different from a model that recommends a treatment. And helping a teacher prepare a lesson is different from interacting directly with a student as a tutor.

So we need to move from general benchmark performance to evaluating the specific use case. What kinds of mistakes does the model make? How consequential are those mistakes? Does it work equally well for different populations? Can it recognize when it doesn’t have enough information, and is there a useful way to defer to a person?

Then there’s the question of evaluating the whole system. If you put a model in front of a clinician or a teacher, does that actually improve their decisions? We can’t assume that having a human involved automatically fixes the model’s errors. People may trust the output too much, or spend so much time checking it that the benefit disappears.

For me, readiness requires evidence in the setting where you intend to deploy it, with outcomes that matter to patients or students. And that evaluation has to continue after deployment, because the model, the population, and the way people use it can all change.

r001.rationale: The response says readiness evaluation should move from general benchmark performance to the specific health care or education use case, including its distinct mistakes and consequences.
